title: Into the Tidyverse: arrange, distinct, select, and mutate

questions.prompt: Why does `flights |> filter(month = 1)` give an error?
choices: A single `=` names an argument; a comparison needs `==`
`filter()` can't be used with the pipe
questions.explain: dplyr says it "detected a named input" and asks "Did you mean `month == 1`?"

questions.prompt: Which dplyr verb sorts the rows of a data frame?
questions.explain: `arrange()` changes the order of the rows, never how many there are.

questions.prompt: Which dplyr verb keeps one row for each unique value?
questions.explain: `distinct(dest)` keeps each destination once.

questions.prompt: Which dplyr verb keeps only the **columns** you name?
questions.explain: `select()` picks columns. `filter()` picks rows.

questions.prompt: Which dplyr verb adds a new column calculated from existing ones?
questions.explain: `mutate(avg_speed = distance / air_time * 60)` adds an `avg_speed` column.

questions.prompt: Which of these verbs work on **rows**?
questions.explain: `filter()`, `distinct()`, and `arrange()` change which rows you have or their order. `select()` and `mutate()` change the columns.

questions.prompt: `flights` has 336,776 rows. How many rows does this return?
questions.explain: There are only three New York City airports in the data: EWR, JFK, and LGA.

questions.prompt: What columns does `flights |> distinct(dest)` return?
questions.explain: `distinct()` keeps only the columns you name (unless you add `.keep_all = TRUE`).

questions.prompt: What does `flights |> distinct(origin, dest)` return?
choices: One row for each unique combination of origin and destination
Every flight, sorted by origin and destination
questions.explain: With more than one column, `distinct()` keeps each unique combination: 224 origin and destination pairs.

questions.prompt: Which question does this code answer?
choices: Where can I fly from JFK?
Which JFK flights were the longest?
questions.explain: `filter()` keeps the JFK flights, and `distinct(dest)` lists each of their destinations once: 70 of them.

questions.prompt: `arrange()` can remove rows from a data frame.
questions.explain: `arrange()` only changes the order of the rows. It never adds or drops any.

questions.prompt: By default, `arrange(dest)` sorts text:
choices: In the order the rows first appear
By how often each value appears
questions.explain: `arrange()` sorts in ascending order by default: A to Z for text, smallest to largest for numbers.

questions.prompt: Complete the code to sort the flights from the longest departure delay to the shortest.
questions.explain: `desc()` sorts in descending order. For numbers, `-dep_delay` works too.

questions.prompt: `arrange(-dest)` sorts the destination codes from Z to A.
questions.explain: The minus sign only works on numbers, and `dest` is text, so R gives an error. Use `arrange(desc(dest))`.

questions.prompt: In what order are the three Atlanta (`ATL`) rows?
choices: The order they first appear in `flights`
questions.explain: `arrange(dest, origin)` sorts by `dest`, then breaks the tie between the three ATL rows with `origin`, A to Z.

questions.prompt: Where do missing values go when you sort with `arrange(desc(dep_delay))`?
questions.explain: Missing values always go last, whichever direction you sort.

questions.prompt: How many rows does this return? (`flights` has 336,776 rows and 19 columns.)
questions.explain: `select()` keeps every row; it only removes columns. The result is 336,776 rows by 4 columns.

questions.prompt: What does `select(-tailnum)` do?
choices: Removes the rows where `tailnum` is missing
questions.explain: A minus sign in `select()` drops that column.

questions.prompt: Complete the code to keep the columns whose names start with `dep`.
questions.explain: `starts_with()` is a selection helper. `ends_with()` and `contains()` work the same way.

questions.prompt: You want only the flights to Raleigh–Durham. Which code is right?
questions.explain: Keeping flights means keeping rows, which is `filter()`'s job. `select()` picks columns.

questions.prompt: Where does `mutate()` put a new column?
choices: At the end of the data frame
questions.explain: New columns go at the end. Use `select()` to bring them into view.

questions.prompt: `air_time` is in minutes. Complete the code to make a column of air time in hours.
questions.explain: Divide minutes by 60 to get hours.

questions.prompt: What is `avg_speed` for a cancelled flight, whose `air_time` is `NA`?
choices: The average of the other flights
questions.explain: Any arithmetic with a missing value gives a missing value.

questions.prompt: What is wrong with `mutate(avg_speed == distance / air_time * 60)`?
choices: `==` compares; naming a new column needs a single `=`
questions.explain: In `mutate()`, `new_name = calculation` uses one `=`. With `==`, R tries to compare `avg_speed` with the speeds, and can't find `avg_speed`.

questions.prompt: Sorting by `avg_speed` shows one flight averaged 703 mph, though airliners cruise at about 550–580 mph. What should you do?
choices: Check it: it's an outlier and may be an error
Report it as the fastest flight
Nothing; the computer can't be wrong
questions.explain: A value far from all the others deserves a second look before you report it. The 65-minute air time for that 762-mile flight may be wrong.

questions.prompt: Put the tiles in order to find the fastest flights, fastest first.
questions.explain: First make the column with `mutate()`, and then sort it, largest first, with `desc()`.

questions.prompt: Put the tiles in order to list, A to Z, the places you can fly from JFK.
questions.explain: Keep the JFK flights, and then list each destination once, and then sort them.

questions.prompt: `distance` (miles) and `air_time` (minutes) are for three flights. Store each flight's average speed in miles per hour in `avg_speed`, in one line, without a loop.
questions.solution:
distance <- c(1400, 762, 4983)
air_time <- c(227, 116, 659)
avg_speed <- distance / air_time * 60
questions.explain: Arithmetic in R is vectorized: `distance / air_time` divides each distance by the air time in the same position. That is what `mutate()` does for every row.

questions.prompt: `dests` holds the destinations of seven flights. Store the **number** of different destinations in `n_dest`. (Hint: `unique()` keeps one of each value.)
questions.explain: `unique()` returns ATL, ORD, RDU, LAX, and `length()` counts them. It is the vector version of `distinct()` followed by `nrow()`.

questions.prompt: Store the delays sorted from **largest to smallest** in `sorted`. (Hint: `sort()` has a `decreasing` argument.)
questions.solution:
delays <- c(12, -3, 45, 0, 7)
sorted <- sort(delays, decreasing = TRUE)
questions.explain: `sort(decreasing = TRUE)` sorts a vector largest first, as `arrange(desc())` does for a data frame.
